blocks.text: GB200 NVL72 的 Ariel 变体为每块 NVIDIA Blackwell GPU 搭配一颗 NVIDIA Grace CPU 和 2 块 NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G 网卡，CPU 与 GPU 的比例为 1:1，使我们能够比业界其他厂商更早地为每块 GPU 部署 800G 的 I/O。我们选择 Ariel，是因为相对于 NVIDIA H100，GB200 NVL72 在几乎所有其他维度上都实现了扩展：FLOPS、HBM 带宽、scale-up 带宽和 scale-up 域规模，而每块 GPU 的 scale-out 带宽原本会停留在 400G。我们预计这种不均衡会损害性能，因此选择了为每块 GPU 提供 800G scale-out 的配置。这也让我们在区域扩展、800G scale-out 变得可用时，拥有更统一的规格。

blocks.text: 在传统 Web 服务中，数据中心网络在实例通常不需要高带宽、高性能以及跨多台服务器紧密锁步协调的服务之间传输请求和响应。大规模 AI 训练需要所有这些特性，这意味着连接它们的网络如今已成为 AI 工作负载的重要组成部分。为最好地解决这一问题，除了连接服务器的标准数据中心网络外，几年前我们还新增了一个基于以太网的专用第二数据网络，称为后端（BE）网络，用于在数据中心建筑内部和跨建筑实现 GPU 到 GPU 的直接通信。

inlines.text: 72-GPU 故障域

blocks.text: 从 H100 世代的 NVL8 架构过渡到 NVL72，从根本上重新定义了我们应对基础设施韧性的方式。在 NVL8 时代，scale-up 域——即通过 NVLink 紧密耦合用于张量并行的 GPU 组——被限制为 8 个单元。借助 NVL72，该域扩展到 72 个 GPU，使故障影响范围扩大 9 倍。

blocks.text: 更大的 scale-up 域正是 NVL72 带宽优势的来源，但它也使 72-GPU 机架成为我们规划容量所依据的分配单元。训练并行性最高效地映射到 2 的幂组大小上，因此每个 NVL72 域运行一个 64-GPU 切片，并将剩余 8 个 GPU 保留为机架内备用。当某个 GPU 发生故障时，备用 GPU 立即接替，因此任务从上一个检查点重启，而不是等待硬件维修，机架也继续留在任务中。机架内冗余将有效机架故障率降至由可能移除整个 pod 的故障所设定的下限；对于更罕见的整机架故障，我们保留约 2% 的额外机架作为储备。对于 32,768 个活跃 GPU 的训练运行，这意味着需要配置 523 个 NVL72 机架，即 37,656 个 GPU，比活跃占用规模高出约 13%。这一余量的大部分（11%）来自 64-of-72 切片几何结构，而不是绝对的可靠性成本。

blocks.text: In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.

blocks.text: At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. blocks.text: The 72-GPU Failure Domain

inlines.text: The 72-GPU Failure Domain

blocks.text: The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

inlines.text: The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

blocks.text: The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

unit of allocation we plan capacity around

. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

blocks.text: Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.

blocks.text: Fault Recovery

inlines.text: Fault Recovery

blocks.text: Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

inlines.text: Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

blocks.text: Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.

We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.

inlines.text: Systematic Reduction of Interruptions

blocks.text: When training frontier models, infrastructure reliability requires a perspective beyond simple availability. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining training momentum without frequent system halts. Within Prometheus, we classify an interruption as any fault — from GPU silicon defects and network fabric anomalies to storage bottlenecks or thermal limits — that forces a job to pause and initiate a recovery cycle.

inlines.text: Maturing Hardware at Fleet Scale

blocks.text: Deploying hundreds of thousands of first-generation accelerators reveals quality issues that are hidden at lower volumes. The GB200 deployment has transformed hardware maturation into a primary engineering discipline for our teams and partners.

blocks.text: Areas of engineering include:

inlines.text: Areas of engineering include:
Rapid Firmware Bundle Deployment:

We built reliable and fast firmware bundle automation, capable of deploying firmware and driver fixes to more than 100k GPUs within a few hours. We’ve brought down the P90 of single-pod upgrade times from more than seven hours in early hardware introduction to two hours. This has let us push rapid fixes for the top interruption categories to our fleet.
Fleet Health:

We correlate telemetry across multi-rack systems and classify every job interruption to guide software fixes, hardware repairs, and replacement decisions. We track MTBI alongside available capacity plus effective training throughput, and have a robust feedback cycle for hardware and software reliability improvements to translate into more productive compute.
Cross-Partner Qualification:
implementing parallel validation with multiple manufacturing partners to ensure consistent quality through continuous feedback from our production fleet.
Automated Signal Screening:
validating over 600,000 NVLink paths using diagnostic stress tests before any production traffic is routed. Even minor defect rates at this scale require proactive identification.
Power Delivery Stress Testing:
investigating how PSU modules and voltage regulators interact under the 1,400W load of individual GPUs to surface failure modes that only appear at high volumes.
Precision Liquid Cooling:
enforcing strict quality gates for cold plate and manifold assembly to maintain optimal junction temperatures and prevent leaks across the fleet.
Fleet Maintenance:
proactive preparation, rapid disposition, prioritization for fix-repair, and prepositioning spares.
Health Checks:
advanced ingestion/burn-in and pre-job health checks used to identify healthy nodes for inclusion in large training jobs.

blocks.text: Optimizing Power and Managing Transients

inlines.text: Optimizing Power and Managing Transients

blocks.text: Maximizing throughput for a given power envelope, minimizing stranded power, and synchronous distributed training introduces a power delivery hurdle. When tens of thousands of GPUs execute compute-heavy phases and communication cycles in unison, they trigger large power transients — sudden load fluctuations of 30-40% within the cluster. Initiating or pausing a major training job can shift loads of more than tens of megawatts in just seconds.

blocks.text: We address this with Dynamo Dimmer, our cluster-wide power management framework that enables intelligent power capping. Instead of hard-stopping workloads, Dimmer gradually adjusts GPU power limits as the cluster nears its electrical ceiling, ensuring training continues uninterrupted. This system is reinforced by rack-level battery backup (BBU) modules that handle immediate spikes, capacitor trays (CBUs) for peak smoothing, facility-level battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deep coordination with utility providers to manage these unique AI profiles.
